chunk_findings.detail: The new `if ev.schema > SCHEMA_VERSION: ... continue` runs *before* the handler lookup and unconditionally, so it bypasses the `strict` path entirely. `State.skipped_kinds` is documented (immediately above `ddflow_versions`, on the same dataclass) as "kind -> count, for events a **non-strict** fold could not interpret… so a caller can refuse to act on a partially-understood log", and the unknown-kind path two lines below only populates it when `strict` is false (it raises otherwise). With this change a `fold(events, strict=True)` over a log containing e.g. `Event(kind="item.created", schema=SCHEMA_VERSION+1, ...)` returns normally instead of raising, and leaves `skipped_kinds` non-empty. A caller that asked for a strict fold precisely to refuse a log it cannot fully interpret now proceeds to act on one, because the "could not interpret" signal is silently demoted to a count.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py:2141 (`_fold` schema guard)

chunk_findings.detail: `v = str(ev.data.get("version", ""))` converts *before* the emptiness guard, so the guard `if not v: return` does not do what it is written to do for a null version: a `ddflow.seen` event with `data={"version": null}` yields `str(None) == "None"`, which is truthy, and is recorded as `st.ddflow_versions["None"]`. That bogus key then participates in `highest_version`'s `max(self.ddflow_versions, key=version_key)`: for the natural tuple-of-int `version_key` this raises `ValueError` on `"None"` (breaking every subsequent fold/skew-guard call), and for a lexicographic key `"None"` sorts above any numeric-leading version, making the log's "highest version" `"None"` and causing the skew guard to refuse every real write. Null/missing version metadata is exactly the case the guard appears intended to drop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py:1826 (`_h_ddflow_seen`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_stamp_and_guard` correctly honours `[upgrade].skew` (`refuse` / `warn` / `off`), but `override_skew` never calls `self._skew_policy()`. Its docstring promises "Nothing is written for policy `off` or `warn` -- those never refuse", yet the code only checks that a skew exists:

```python
facts = stamp_facts(events, self.agent_id, version)
if not facts.highest or not is_older(version, facts.highest):
    return None
if facts.override is not None:
    return facts.override
if not reason:
    raise SkewRefused(...)
ev = self._write(SKEW_OVERRIDDEN_KIND, ...)
```

Concrete failure: set `[upgrade].skew = warn` (or `off`), have a log whose highest stamp is newer than the running ddflow, and invoke the CLI/MCP with `--allow-older-version --reason "..."`. The guard would not have refused (warn/off), so no override is needed; nevertheless `facts.highest` is truthy and `is_older(version, facts.highest)` is true, so a `skew.overridden` event is appended with the current session id and reason. That event is shown in replay/history/doctor, is listed by `ddflow upgrade`, and — per the stated intent — "marks the session's events as from an older version", i.e. the log is polluted with a session-scoped override record that the operator's policy explicitly said should not exist. The same path also means a `warn`-mode user who defensively passes the flag gets a permanent, misleading audit entry. The fix is to consult `_skew_policy()` (and return `None` for `warn`/`off`) before writing the override event, as the docstring already claims.

chunk_findings.detail: The override is recorded unconditionally whenever the MCP caller supplies the `allow_older_version` argument, with no check that the log is actually skewed. Given a project whose log carries no stamp newer than the running ddflow, a client that passes `allow_older_version` (e.g. pre-emptively, or a stale harness that always sets it) drives `self._override_skew(allow_older, agent)` into writing a `skew.overridden` event and marking the session's events as "written by an older ddflow" even though the skew guard would never have refused the call. That is factually wrong provenance: those events are then shown as from an older version in replay/history/doctor and listed by `ddflow upgrade`, and the log gets a `skew.overridden` entry that records an override which never happened. The same unconditional call also means the event is emitted on every write tool invocation for the session rather than once, so a session making N writes with the flag appends N `skew.overridden` events instead of the single recorded override the intent describes. The override should be recorded only when a skew refusal actually occurred (or only when the log's highest stamp really exceeds the running version), not merely because the argument was present.

chunk_findings.detail: `sorted(st.ddflow_versions)` sorts the version strings lexicographically, not by version order. Given a log touched by `0.1.9` and then `0.1.10` (the exact ordering that matters for a "highest version seen"/skew feature), this emits `"seen": ["0.1.10", "0.1.9"]`, which reverses the true historical order and contradicts the semantics of `highest` in the same object. The rest of this change carefully computes the highest version with semver-aware comparison, so the `seen` list is the one place that is ordered by raw string comparison; any consumer that reads it (replay/history/doctor) will show the versions out of order for the common `x.y.10` vs `x.y.9` case. Sorting with a version-key (e.g. a semver parse, or `sorted(..., key=parse_version)`) would produce the expected `["0.1.9", "0.1.10"]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting.py:176 (`data["ddflow_version"]["seen"]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises the fold works in "any order", but `highest` is selected with a strict `>` over `version_key`, so among stamps that have the same comparable key but different spelling, whichever one is encountered first wins as the string value. Given the events `ddflow.seen version="0.2.0"` and `ddflow.seen version="v0.2.0"` (the `v?` in `_VERSION_HEAD` shows prefixed stamps are expected, and both keys are `(0, 2, 0)`), folding in one order yields `highest == "0.2.0"`, folding the same two events reversed yields `highest == "v0.2.0"`. Because the override is matched by string equality — `d.get("log_version") == highest` — an override whose writer recorded `log_version="0.2.0"` from one fold is silently ignored when the same log is folded in the other order, and the older ddflow that was just authorized is refused again with exit 3. The result of `stamp_facts` (and thus of the refusal decision and of `StampFacts.override`) therefore depends on input order, contradicting the function's contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py:stamp_facts

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key` compares tuples of unequal length, and a shorter tuple that is a prefix of a longer one compares as smaller, so two spellings of the same release are not equal. `is_older("0.2", "0.2.0")` returns `(0,2) < (0,2,0)` → `True`, and the guard will refuse a write from a `0.2`-versioned ddflow against a log stamped `0.2.0` (or `1.0` vs `1.0.0`), exiting 3 with "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0" even though no newer release exists. PEP-440-equivalent releases with different component counts (`0.2` and `0.2.0`) are the same release, so `is_older`'s "strictly older release" contract is violated; padding both keys to equal length (or a real version parser) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py:is_older / version_key

chunk_findings.detail: The new schema guard is placed *before* the existing `handler is None` / `if strict:` path, and it unconditionally increments `st.skipped_kinds` and `continue`s. But the `skipped_kinds` contract added in this same diff is explicitly scoped to non-strict folds: "kind -> count, for events a non-strict fold could not interpret ... so a caller can refuse to act on a partially-understood log." With `strict=True`, the pre-existing behavior was that an event whose kind has no handler (e.g. an event from a *future* ddflow) is refused rather than folded. Concrete input: fold (with `strict=True`) an event `{"kind": "session.future", "schema": 99, "data": {}}` where `SCHEMA_VERSION` is the current value and `"session.future"` is not in `HANDLERS`. Previously the `handler is None` / `if strict:` branch fired and the fold refused; now the new branch at line 2141 matches first, writes `skipped_kinds["session.future (schema 99)"] = 1`, and continues. So a strict caller that relies on an exception (and on `skipped_kinds` being empty in strict mode) to detect that it must not act on a partially-understood log now silently proceeds and operates on State derived from events it could not interpret. If the intent is genuinely that future-schema events behave "like skipped kinds", the branch must route through the same strict/non-strict handling (or run after the handler lookup) instead of short-circuiting it.

chunk_findings.detail: `override_skew` never consults `[upgrade].skew`, despite its own docstring promising "Nothing is written for policy `off` or `warn` -- those never refuse." The method only bails out when there is no skew (`if not facts.highest or not is_older(version, facts.highest): return None`); otherwise it checks `facts.override` and, failing that, writes `SKEW_OVERRIDDEN_KIND` unconditionally after the reason check. Concretely: configure `[upgrade].skew = warn`, have a log stamped by a newer version, and invoke the override path (e.g. a wrapper that always passes `--allow-older-version --reason "ci"`, or `ddflow upgrade --allow-older-version`). The write was never refused, yet a `skew.overridden` event is appended (and returned/listed by `ddflow upgrade`), polluting the log with an override that corresponds to no refusal. Worse, that event persists: if the operator later tightens the config back to `skew = refuse`, `facts.override` is non-`None` and `_stamp_and_guard` will silently authorize the older writer with `OLDER_MARK` instead of refusing, so the recorded override outlives the `warn`/`off` period it was never needed for. The policy check that the docstring describes ("those never refuse") is simply missing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py `override_skew`

chunk_findings.detail:
The new flag pair documents `--reason` as a hard precondition ("needs --reason, is recorded"; the operator decision lists the override as `--allow-older-version --reason`), but the code never enforces it. For an input like `ddflow --allow-older-version write ...` (no top-level `--reason`, and a subcommand whose own `--reason` defaults to `None`/unset), the expression

    reason = getattr(args, "skew_reason", "") or str(getattr(args, "reason", "") or "")

evaluates to `""`, and `ctx.log.override_skew("")` is invoked anyway. The CLI then proceeds into `args.fn`, so the skew guard is overridden with an empty, unrecorded justification — exactly the "operator's insistence" audit record the change says is required. There is no path in this diff that rejects `--allow-older-version` when no reason was supplied (and the fallback to `getattr(args, "reason", ...)` is `""` for every command that has no own `--reason`, so `--reason` is effectively optional). If `override_skew` instead signals "empty reason ⇒ not applied" by returning `None`, the same input prints the misleading `"ddflow: no version skew; --allow-older-version ignored"` and the subsequent write is refused with the "upgrade ddflow-mcp" message rather than a missing-reason error; either way the documented precondition is not honored by this code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py:1489 (`--allow-older-version` / `--reason` handling in `main`)

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key("0.2.0rc1") == (0, 2, 0)` collapses a pre-release onto its base release, so `is_older("0.2.0rc1", "0.2.0")` returns `False`. Concrete failure: a log whose highest `ddflow.seen` stamp is `"0.2.0"` (written by the released build) plus a running `ddflow.__version__ == "0.2.0rc1"` (an earlier build). The guard should refuse the write (exit 3, "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0"), but because both versions map to `(0, 2, 0)` the comparison is `False`, the refusal is skipped, and the older build's events are appended. The same collapse also makes `rc1` and `rc2` of one release indistinguishable, so an older rc can write onto a log stamped by a newer rc. The test asserts this lossy mapping instead of ordering pre-releases before the final release, so the skew guard silently misses pre-release skew.

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key` orders pre-releases by the *first integer found in the suffix* while completely discarding the suffix *label*, so two pre-releases of the same numeric version get ordered by their trailing number instead of by the PEP-440 label order (dev < a < b < rc < release). Concretely, `version_key("0.2.0.dev5")` returns `((0, 2), (0, 5))` and `version_key("0.2.0rc1")` returns `((0, 2), (0, 1))`, so `is_older("0.2.0rc1", "0.2.0.dev5")` is `True` even though `rc1` is *newer* than `dev5`. Given a log whose highest stamp is `0.2.0.dev5` (a ddflow version the docstring itself cites as realistic) and a running ddflow `0.2.0rc1`, the skew guard will refuse the first write with exit 3 and "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0.dev5" — a legitimate write blocked. The mirror case is equally wrong in the other direction: `version_key("0.2.0a1")` and `version_key("0.2.0rc1")` are both `((0, 2), (0, 1))`, so they compare *equal*; a log stamped by `0.2.0rc1` will not refuse a write by the older `0.2.0a1`, so the guard silently fails open (and fold's `(version_key(v), v) > (version_key(highest), highest)` tie-break then selects the "highest" string lexicographically, which for equal keys is arbitrary with respect to true version order). The pre-release comparison needs to incorporate the label (e.g. dev/a/b/rc) before the trailing number, otherwise `devN > rcN` and `aN == rcN`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff deletes the `skew_facts()` method entirely:

```python
-    def skew_facts(self):
-        """`core.events.StampFacts` for this agent under the RUNNING version."""
-        return stamp_facts(self._all_events(), self.agent_id, running_version())
```

but nothing in this diff replaces it, and the two consumers that need exactly that value live a few lines below in unchanged code: `_stamp_and_guard` (the write-time skew guard, whose body spans the unshown lines 704–737) and the override recorder (whose hidden setup lines, ~747, are immediately followed by the shown `return None` / `if facts.override is not None:` block). Both obtain their `StampFacts` via `self.skew_facts()`; with the method removed they raise `AttributeError: 'Log' object has no attribute 'skew_facts'`. Concretely, the first write to any log — the basic append path that runs the guard before stamping `ddflow.seen` — now dies with an `AttributeError` traceback instead of either stamping the running version or refusing an older one with exit 3 and the "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X" message, so the entire skew feature this change introduces is unreachable. Any other caller (e.g. doctor/replay, which the intent says name versions) hits the same `AttributeError`. If the method was meant to be inlined at its call sites, those call-site edits are missing from the change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py (~line 696, removed `Log.skew_facts`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion was widened from the specific file `.ddflow/local/clone-id` to the entire directory `.ddflow/local`:

```python
assert not (repo / ".ddflow" / "local").exists()
```

But the same test performs a real write two lines earlier — `L.EventLog(repo, "someone").append("task.added", "X1", {"title": "t"})` — and the feature under review defines a *local marker* at exactly `.ddflow/local/seen.json` that is written by this machine on the first write after a version change (equivalently, the first write against an unstamped log, which is what a freshly-created test repo is). That write creates the `.ddflow/local` directory, so `(repo/".ddflow"/"local").exists()` is true and the assertion fails, even though the property the test is actually about — that a *read* (`L.EventLog(repo).read_all()`) must not mint a new `clone-id` — still holds. The previous, file-scoped assertion (`... / "clone-id"`) passed precisely because the directory may exist while no clone-id file is written. To keep testing read-side non-mutation, the assertion should stay scoped to `local/clone-id` (or to whatever specific file the read must not create), not the whole directory.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_log_lamport_merge.py:239 (the changed assert)

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key` compares tuples of unequal length, and a shorter tuple that is a prefix of a longer one compares as smaller, so two spellings of the same release are not equal. `is_older("0.2", "0.2.0")` returns `(0,2) < (0,2,0)` → `True`, and the guard will refuse a write from a `0.2`-versioned ddflow against a log stamped `0.2.0` (or `1.0` vs `1.0.0`), exiting 3 with "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0" even though no newer release exists. PEP-440-equivalent releases with different component counts (`0.2` and `0.2.0`) are the same release, so `is_older`'s "strictly older release" contract is violated; padding both keys to equal length (or a real version parser) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py:is_older / version_key

chunk_findings.detail: The new schema guard is placed *before* the existing `handler is None` / `if strict:` path, and it unconditionally increments `st.skipped_kinds` and `continue`s. But the `skipped_kinds` contract added in this same diff is explicitly scoped to non-strict folds: "kind -> count, for events a non-strict fold could not interpret ... so a caller can refuse to act on a partially-understood log." With `strict=True`, the pre-existing behavior was that an event whose kind has no handler (e.g. an event from a *future* ddflow) is refused rather than folded. Concrete input: fold (with `strict=True`) an event `{"kind": "session.future", "schema": 99, "data": {}}` where `SCHEMA_VERSION` is the current value and `"session.future"` is not in `HANDLERS`. Previously the `handler is None` / `if strict:` branch fired and the fold refused; now the new branch at line 2141 matches first, writes `skipped_kinds["session.future (schema 99)"] = 1`, and continues. So a strict caller that relies on an exception (and on `skipped_kinds` being empty in strict mode) to detect that it must not act on a partially-understood log now silently proceeds and operates on State derived from events it could not interpret. If the intent is genuinely that future-schema events behave "like skipped kinds", the branch must route through the same strict/non-strict handling (or run after the handler lookup) instead of short-circuiting it.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/core/model.py:2141 (the `if ev.schema > SCHEMA_VERSION:` branch in the fold)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py:2141 (the `if ev.schema > SCHEMA_VERSION:` branch in the fold)

chunk_findings.detail: `override_skew` never consults `[upgrade].skew`, despite its own docstring promising "Nothing is written for policy `off` or `warn` -- those never refuse." The method only bails out when there is no skew (`if not facts.highest or not is_older(version, facts.highest): return None`); otherwise it checks `facts.override` and, failing that, writes `SKEW_OVERRIDDEN_KIND` unconditionally after the reason check. Concretely: configure `[upgrade].skew = warn`, have a log stamped by a newer version, and invoke the override path (e.g. a wrapper that always passes `--allow-older-version --reason "ci"`, or `ddflow upgrade --allow-older-version`). The write was never refused, yet a `skew.overridden` event is appended (and returned/listed by `ddflow upgrade`), polluting the log with an override that corresponds to no refusal. Worse, that event persists: if the operator later tightens the config back to `skew = refuse`, `facts.override` is non-`None` and `_stamp_and_guard` will silently authorize the older writer with `OLDER_MARK` instead of refusing, so the recorded override outlives the `warn`/`off` period it was never needed for. The policy check that the docstring describes ("those never refuse") is simply missing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py `override_skew`

chunk_findings.detail:
The new flag pair documents `--reason` as a hard precondition ("needs --reason, is recorded"; the operator decision lists the override as `--allow-older-version --reason`), but the code never enforces it. For an input like `ddflow --allow-older-version write ...` (no top-level `--reason`, and a subcommand whose own `--reason` defaults to `None`/unset), the expression

    reason = getattr(args, "skew_reason", "") or str(getattr(args, "reason", "") or "")

evaluates to `""`, and `ctx.log.override_skew("")` is invoked anyway. The CLI then proceeds into `args.fn`, so the skew guard is overridden with an empty, unrecorded justification — exactly the "operator's insistence" audit record the change says is required. There is no path in this diff that rejects `--allow-older-version` when no reason was supplied (and the fallback to `getattr(args, "reason", ...)` is `""` for every command that has no own `--reason`, so `--reason` is effectively optional). If `override_skew` instead signals "empty reason ⇒ not applied" by returning `None`, the same input prints the misleading `"ddflow: no version skew; --allow-older-version ignored"` and the subsequent write is refused with the "upgrade ddflow-mcp" message rather than a missing-reason error; either way the documented precondition is not honored by this code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py:1489 (`--allow-older-version` / `--reason` handling in `main`)

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key("0.2.0rc1") == (0, 2, 0)` collapses a pre-release onto its base release, so `is_older("0.2.0rc1", "0.2.0")` returns `False`. Concrete failure: a log whose highest `ddflow.seen` stamp is `"0.2.0"` (written by the released build) plus a running `ddflow.__version__ == "0.2.0rc1"` (an earlier build). The guard should refuse the write (exit 3, "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0"), but because both versions map to `(0, 2, 0)` the comparison is `False`, the refusal is skipped, and the older build's events are appended. The same collapse also makes `rc1` and `rc2` of one release indistinguishable, so an older rc can write onto a log stamped by a newer rc. The test asserts this lossy mapping instead of ordering pre-releases before the final release, so the skew guard silently misses pre-release skew.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_upgrade_stamp.py::test_versions_compare_as_numbers_not_text

chunk_findings.detail: `version_key` orders pre-releases purely by the first integer found in the suffix, ignoring the pre-release identifier itself, so it mis-orders exactly the two forms the new docstring names (`rc`, `dev`). Given the log's highest stamp `0.2.0rc1`, `version_key("0.2.0.dev3")` is `((0,2),(0,3))` and `version_key("0.2.0rc1")` is `((0,2),(0,1))`, so a writer at `0.2.0.dev3` (older than `rc1` per PEP 440 / release ordering) is judged *newer* and `is_older` returns False: the skew guard allows the write instead of refusing with exit 3. The reverse is also a user-visible false refusal: with highest `0.2.0.dev3` and a running version `0.2.0rc1`, `version_key` makes the newer `rc1` the smaller key, so a current binary is refused and told to "upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.2.0.dev3". Same class of error for `0.2.0a5` vs `0.2.0b1` (5 > 1, so `a5` is reported newer). Because the fold's `highest` selection uses the same key, `ddflow status --json`/doctor also report the wrong highest stamp for such a log.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py:version_key (`pre = re.search(r"\d+", rest)` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The fold deliberately keeps multiple spellings of one version (its comparison is `(version_key(v), v)`, with the comment "two spellings of one version resolve the same way in any order"), but `reporting.py` sorts with `key=version_key` alone, i.e. it drops the same text tie-breaker. Two distinct strings with equal keys, e.g. `"0.2"` and `"0.2.0"` (or `"0.1.0"`/`"0.1"`), are therefore ordered by whatever order `st.ddflow_versions` yields. Since that state is written with `sorted(...)` it is set-like, and set iteration over strings is hash-randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so `ddflow_version.seen` can flip between `["0.2","0.2.0"]` and `["0.2.0","0.2"]` across runs, where the old `sorted(st.ddflow_versions)` was a stable total order. The fix is the same tie-break the fold uses, `key=lambda v: (version_key(v), v)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting.py:179 (`sorted(st.ddflow_versions, key=version_key)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff deletes `Log.skew_facts`, which was the single wrapper producing `stamp_facts(self._all_events(), self.agent_id, running_version())` — i.e. the `core.events.StampFacts` value (`.running`, `.highest`, `.override`) that the skew guard runs on. It sat directly above `_stamp_and_guard` precisely because that method needs it to decide whether the running version is older than the log's highest stamp, and `record_skew_override` (whose body still derives `facts` and dereferences `facts.override` in this very hunk, at the `if facts.override is not None:` line) consumes the same value. No replacement computation is introduced in this diff, so any caller now hits `AttributeError: 'Log' object has no attribute 'skew_facts'`. Concretely: running a write from an older ddflow-mcp against a log stamped by a newer version (the exact scenario described in the intent) no longer reaches the exit-3 refusal / `upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X` path — the guard code faults before it can compare stamps; likewise `--allow-older-version --reason ...` can never emit the `skew.overridden` event, because the function that produces `facts.override` is gone.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py — removal of `Log.skew_facts`

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion was broadened from `not (repo / ".ddflow" / "local" / "clone-id").exists()` to `not (repo / ".ddflow" / "local").exists()`. Per the intent, this change introduces a *local marker* at exactly `.ddflow/local/seen.json` that is written by the write path ("gets stamped on first write", "Local marker .ddflow/local/seen.json = last version THIS machine acted under"). The test body performs a write before the assertion:

    L.EventLog(repo, "someone").append("task.added", "X1", {"title": "t"})
    L._AGENT_ID_CACHE.clear()
    L.EventLog(repo).read_all()
    assert not (repo / ".ddflow" / "local").exists()

Because the `append` above is the first write, the version-stamp logic creates `.ddflow/local/seen.json`, so `.ddflow/local` exists and the assertion fails. The previous assertion (a single file `clone-id`) correctly ignored the new marker file; the new directory-wide assertion cannot, so this test goes from passing to deterministically failing for any run that writes to the log. To keep the original intent (a read must not touch `local`), the assertion must name the specific file it cares about, not the whole directory the feature now populates.
